results.title: An Unspeakable Crime: The Prosecution and Persecution of Leo Frank by Elaine Marie Alphin
results.creator: Elaine Marie Alphin
results.description: An Unspeakable Crime : A Visually Impressive but Unreliable Introduction to the Leo Frank Case A Critical Review of Its Facts, Sources, Omissions, and Extreme Pro-Frank Framing An Unspeakable Crime: The Prosecution and Persecution of Leo Frank is clearly written, attractively designed, and filled with an impressive collection of historical photographs. As a physical book, it is one of the better-produced introductions to the Leo Frank case. Many of its photographs are reproduced with unusual clarity, its chapters move quickly, and its vocabulary is accessible to the young readers for whom it was written. Those qualities make the book inviting. They do not make it reliable. This is not a balanced history of Mary Phagan’s murder, Leo Frank’s trial, or the long controversy that followed. It occupies the extreme pro-Frank end of the literature, alongside the works of Leonard Dinnerstein, Harry Golden, and Charles and Louise Samuels. The book begins with Frank as an innocent victim, interprets the evidence through that assumption, and ends by presenting his innocence as a moral conclusion rather than a disputed historical claim. The basic problem is not that the book argues for Frank’s innocence. A writer is entitled to reach that conclusion. The problem is that the conclusion arrives before the investigation. Evidence favorable to Frank is readily accepted, even when it first appeared decades later, rests upon hearsay, or cannot be tested. Evidence supporting the verdict is treated with suspicion, reduced to prejudice, or left out of the narrative. The result is a book that should not be used as a first introduction to the case. A reader who begins here will receive a carefully constructed story of persecution, but not a complete account of the evidence heard by the jury. The Verdict Was Reached Before the Research Began The book’s title announces its position before the first chapter opens. The phrase “an unspeakable crime” originally appeared in Atlanta Mayor James Woodward’s defense of Frank’s lynching as punishment for Mary Phagan’s murder. The book recasts those words so that the “unspeakable crime” gradually becomes not Mary’s murder, but the prosecution and persecution of Leo Frank. Even the dedication frames the project as an effort to expose injustice. There is no corresponding indication that the author intends to determine whether the jury had legitimate reasons for convicting Frank. The moral identities have already been assigned. Frank is the victim. The police, prosecutor, witnesses, jurors, courts, and people of Georgia are placed under suspicion. The author’s note at the back of the book confirms how early this interpretation took hold. Before undertaking substantial archival research, the author read Leonard Dinnerstein’s The Leo Frank Case , listened to the score of the musical Parade , and watched the television dramatization The Murder of Mary Phagan . She writes that she was already astonished that such a “travesty of justice” had occurred. That admission is revealing. She did not begin by asking whether Frank was guilty, whether the evidence was sufficient, or whether the modern innocence narrative had accurately represented the trial. She entered the archives after absorbing three major pro-Frank interpretations and after deciding that the case represented a miscarriage of justice. Her research then concentrated heavily upon collections devoted to Frank, his family, his supporters, and Atlanta’s Jewish community. She handled love letters between Leo and Lucille, read sympathetic correspondence sent to the family, examined Frank family photographs, and studied Lucille’s descriptions of her husband’s imprisonment and death. By the end of the process, she writes that she felt personally entrusted to tell “their story.” That emotional connection is understandable. It also helps explain the book’s imbalance. The author became deeply attached to Frank and Lucille, while Mary Phagan remained largely a figure whose death initiated Frank’s ordeal. The book is therefore best understood as advocacy illustrated with archival photographs. Its research is real, but the research is filtered through a conclusion established beforehand. A System of Unequal Skepticism The book uses two different standards of proof. When evidence points toward Frank, the police are assumed to have distorted it, witnesses are presumed to have lied, and prosecutors are accused of coaching, threatening, or manipulating them. When evidence favors Frank, the requirements become far more relaxed. A decades-late recollection, an untested affidavit, a supposed confession reported by a third party, an unverifiable newspaper claimant, or a disputed memoir may be treated as credible. This creates a closed argumentative system. Evidence against Frank is rejected because the system was corrupt. Evidence that the system was corrupt is then established by the fact that it produced evidence against Frank. Under that method, almost nothing can count against him. His nervousness is misunderstood. His changing explanations are innocent confusion. His absence from the office is declared irrelevant. His unsworn statement is treated as the speech of a restrained intellectual. The witnesses against him are frightened, coached, greedy, racist, dishonest, or caught in mass hysteria. The same generosity is not extended to Jim Conley, Newt Lee, Minola McKnight, Albert McKnight, Hugh Dorsey, the jurors, or the judges who reviewed the case. A sound history asks the same questions of every witness and every source. This book does not. Mary Phagan Is Misdescribed from the Beginning The first chapter introduces Mary through a mixture of fact, speculation, and language that is strangely sexualized for a book aimed at young readers. On page 6, the thirteen-year-old girl is described as having an “already well-developed figure” and as looking forward to “innocent flirting with boys.” Neither description is necessary to explain her movements on April 26, 1913. Both encourage the reader to imagine her through adult sexuality before the crime has even been introduced. The book then makes basic errors about Mary’s family. On page 10, it states that Mary was born in Marietta and that her father died there. Mary Anne Phagan was born in Florence, Alabama, on June 1, 1899. Her biological father died before she was born, making her a posthumous child. Her mother was Frances Benton Phagan Coleman, commonly called Fannie. The book repeatedly calls her “Frannie,” a name unsupported by the family record. It also gives the impression that Frances remarried soon after her first husband’s death and that Mary was raised by John Coleman. Frances did not marry Coleman until 1912, when Mary was approximately twelve years old. Mary had spent nearly her entire childhood without a father in the household. The book also claims that John Coleman used a neighbor’s telephone to call police after midnight when Mary failed to return home. The surviving family account does not support that assertion. The family searched and waited through the night. At approximately 5:30 the following morning, Helen Ferguson arrived and told them that Mary had been found dead. These may appear to be small biographical details, but they expose an important imbalance. A book devoted to correcting supposed falsehoods about Frank should first establish the basic facts about Mary accurately. The treatment of her mother also reflects the larger problem. Frances Phagan’s grief, her courtroom experience, and the psychological destruction caused by her daughter’s murder receive little sustained attention. Lucille Frank’s emotions, letters, fears, losses, and loyalty receive pages of sympathetic narration. Mary is present, but Frank is the emotional subject. The Bite-Mark Story Is Presented as Fact Without Contemporary Evidence One of the book’s most serious errors appears on page 11, where it states that one of Mary’s shoulders had been bitten. The same story reappears later as alleged proof that Frank could not have been the killer. No bite marks were documented in the contemporary autopsy testimony, the official Brief of Evidence , the coroner’s proceedings, the police evidence, or the major Atlanta newspaper reports from 1913. The story appears to derive from Pierre van Paassen’s 1964 memoir, To Number Our Days . Van Paassen claimed that during a 1922 visit to Atlanta he saw photographs of bite marks and dental evidence showing that Frank’s teeth did not match them. He also claimed that the marks had been X-rayed and preserved in a court file. The book does not explain that this story appeared more than fifty years after the murder. It does not ask why no doctor, undertaker, police officer, prosecutor, defense attorney, trial witness, newspaper reporter, appellate lawyer, or clemency investigator mentioned such decisive evidence at the time. It also does not explain how bite impressions in human flesh were supposedly X-rayed for dental comparison in 1913, or why the photographs and dental records vanished without leaving a trace in the trial record. Instead, the story grows stronger as the book proceeds. By pages 132 and 133, it has developed into a claim that Hugh Dorsey knew the dental evidence excluded Frank and deliberately suppressed it. A doubtful memoir has been transformed into prosecutorial misconduct. This is not responsible source criticism. It is the acceptance of a late legend because the legend supports the desired conclusion. The bite-mark claim also appears in other pro-Frank writings, including later treatments that cite van Paassen. Repetition does not create corroboration when the writers are repeating the same unsupported source. Imagined Thoughts Are Used as Historical Evidence The book frequently tells readers what historical figures supposedly thought, feared, intended, or felt without identifying evidence for those inner states. On page 11, it imagines that the officers who saw Mary’s body were especially angry because the factory was operated by a Northern businessman. On pages 15 through 20, the narration repeatedly enters Frank’s mind, explaining his uneasiness, reluctance, confusion, outrage, and private reasoning. On pages 23 and 24, the book says that nearly any Northern businessman would have been regarded as an enemy in Atlanta. It then describes Frank’s facial features, height, weight, mouth, glasses, and physical appearance as the image of a “calculating Yankee.” This is an odd method for a book condemning prejudice. The author criticizes 1913 Atlantans for allegedly reading guilt into Frank’s appearance, then supplies an elaborate description of how his face and body supposedly appeared to them. Later chapters continue this practice. The book tells readers what Dorsey needed politically, what the jury felt, why factory girls testified, what the crowd believed, why witnesses lied, how Frank’s calmness was misunderstood, and what Lucille must have thought after the verdict. Historical narrative often requires reasonable inference. This book repeatedly crosses the line from inference into invention. Frank’s Family History Is Embellished The portrait of Frank’s background is filled with undocumented or weakly supported claims. On page 23, the book says that Frank’s father, Rudolph, had been forced to retire after a railway accident and that the family lived on interest from an injury settlement. No contemporary documentation is supplied. The claim appears to trace back to Arthur Burton Rascoe’s 1947 booklet, where it was also presented without supporting evidence. The 1910 federal census continued to list Rudolph Frank as a salesman. When Rachel Frank testified, she explained her husband’s absence from the trial by saying that he was nervous and physically broken down from work. She did not describe him as a retired railway accident victim living upon a settlement. The same page says that Frank’s uncle Moses had fought for the Confederacy. This assertion was introduced publicly by defense attorney Reuben Arnold in October 1913, but no reliable Confederate service record has been produced. Frank later denied the story. The Selig family is described as part of Atlanta’s “high society.” Lucille’s father was a traveling salesman for the West Disinfecting Company and had previously worked in the liquor trade. The family was respectable and financially comfortable, but the grander description contributes to the book’s recurring effort to surround Frank with refinement, status, and moral prestige. Page 25 says that Lucille proudly announced a pregnancy in the spring of 1913. Page 85 then treats her miscarriage as a secret known only to the immediate family. The account appears to depend upon interviews conducted more than seventy years later. The extensive surviving correspondence between Leo, Lucille, and their relatives contains no clear contemporary reference to the pregnancy or miscarriage. The event may have occurred. The evidence does not justify narrating it with the certainty used here. The book also portrays Frank and his family as relatively poor. Frank earned approximately $150 per month as superintendent of the National Pencil Company, a substantial professional salary in 1913. He had traveled to Europe twice, studied pencil manufacturing in Germany, belonged to social and fraternal organizations, and had access to a powerful legal defense network. Calling him poor may make him appear less privileged against the factory workers who testified against him, but it does not fit comfortably with the economic record. Newt Lee’s Full Story Is Missing The treatment of Newt Lee is one of the clearest examples of how the book’s racial framework displaces the actual evidence. Pages 12 through 14 present Lee’s arrest mainly as the predictable action of White Southern officers who saw an elderly Black man and assumed he must be guilty. The book then quotes a later account claiming that the police decided “a Negro’s blood would not suffice” and therefore turned toward a White suspect. That theory is internally confused. The book first condemns the police for reflexively arresting a Black man, then accuses the same police of rejecting a Black suspect because convicting him would not be impressive enough. More important, it does not fully explain why investigators questioned Lee. Lee was the night watchman. He was alone in the factory when Mary’s body was discovered. He found the body and telephoned police. The two murder notes found beside Mary appeared to point toward a “night witch,” an apparent attempt to implicate the night watchman. His time slip contained missing punches. A blood-marked shirt was later discovered at his home. The book also omits one of the most suspicious parts of Lee’s account. Frank had told him to report early on Saturday, April 26, at 4:00 p.m. instead of his usual 5:00 p.m. starting time. When Lee arrived, he encountered a locked door. Frank admitted him, but then sent him away and told him not to remain inside the factory. He instructed Lee to return at 6:00 p.m., one hour later than Lee normally began work. That sequence does not prove Frank killed Mary or attempted to frame Lee. It does, however, require analysis. The alteration of Lee’s schedule, the murder notes, the time slip, and the shirt form a connected body of evidence. A serious introduction should place those facts together and allow readers to decide what they mean. Instead, the book turns Lee mainly into the first victim of racist policing and then moves forward. The Murder Notes Are Never Fully Confronted The two notes found beside Mary’s body are reproduced prominently, but their strategic purpose is not seriously examined. Jim Conley admitted writing them. The deeper question is who designed their message and why. The notes attempted to place blame upon a tall Black night watchman. Conley denied knowing Newt Lee. Frank knew Lee, supervised him, knew his schedule, and knew that Lee would enter the building that evening. Frank also knew that Lee was likely to discover the body. The book concentrates upon Conley’s handwriting and his changing statements. It does not sufficiently distinguish handwriting from authorship. A person may physically write words dictated or devised by someone else. Nor does the book adequately ask why Conley, acting as a lone killer, would write two elaborate notes pointing toward a night watchman he claimed not to know. The notes fit more naturally into a plan created by someone familiar with Lee, his duties, his appearance, and his expected arrival. Arthur Burton Rascoe, Francis Xavier Busch, Mary Phagan-Kean, and the Historical Research Department of the Nation of Islam have all examined this distinction between Conley as writer and another person as intellectual author. Their conclusions should be tested against the primary record, but the question cannot be dismissed by proving that Conley held the pencil. The Physical Evidence Is Broken into Harmless Fragments The prosecution’s case was cumulative. No single item carried the entire weight. The evidence drew its force from the way the separate pieces connected. The book weakens that structure by discussing each item separately and supplying an innocent possibility for it. The hair found on the second-floor metal-room lathe is treated as uncertain. The suspected blood spots are reduced to contamination or an unidentified source. The basement evidence is separated from the second-floor evidence. The elevator route is not fairly reconstructed. The drag trail, the cord ligature, the body’s position, the uncrushed parasol, the basement debris, and the suspected blood near the dressing room never receive the combined analysis they require. On page 66, the book acknowledges that chemist Claude Smith testified that wood chips taken from the metal room contained blood. It immediately emphasizes his admission that the blood could not be identified as human and could theoretically have belonged to a mouse. That possibility existed. It does not erase the location of the stains, the hair, the testimony about Mary’s movements, or the prosecution’s theory that the assault occurred on the second floor. This is a recurring technique. Each item is isolated until it appears trivial. The reader is rarely invited to view the evidence as a pattern. A circumstantial case cannot be evaluated by asking whether every individual fact has some possible innocent explanation. The proper question is whether the combined facts form a coherent explanation and whether the competing theory explains them better. Monteen Stover Is Declared Irrelevant Too Quickly Monteen Stover testified that she entered the factory between approximately 12:05 and 12:10 p.m. to collect her pay. She went to Frank’s office and found it empty. This was important because Frank’s early account placed him in the office during that period. The prosecution argued that Stover entered during the interval when Frank had gone into the metal room with Mary. The book later declares Stover’s testimony irrelevant because a streetcar conductor placed Mary’s arrival later than the prosecution claimed. That conclusion is far too absolute. Streetcar testimony involved estimates, routes, stops, and recollections developed months after the event. The defense evidence complicated the prosecution’s timeline, but it did not cause Stover’s observation to vanish. Frank still had to explain why his office was empty during a period when he had said he was there. In his March 1914 jailhouse interview, Frank revisited this problem and suggested that he might have gone to the toilet in the metal room. That statement was significant because the prosecution had placed the murder in or near that area. The book does not give this development the weight it deserves. Lemmie Quinn’s visit is also treated as though it supplied an alibi. It did not account for the entire noon period. A visitor who saw Frank at one point cannot establish his presence during every minute before and after the visit. The proper analysis requires a minute-by-minute reconstruction. The book prefers a broad declaration that the prosecution’s timeline had collapsed. The Medical Disagreement Is Turned into Exoneration Dr. Henry Harris testified about Mary’s facial injuries, the condition of the food in her stomach, and signs of violence in the genital area. Based upon digestion, he estimated that she died approximately thirty to forty-five minutes after eating. Dr. J. W. Hurt disagreed with parts of Harris’s interpretation, particularly concerning genital injury. Defense experts also challenged the digestion estimate. That created a medical dispute. It did not “render the prosecution’s entire timeline invalid,” as the book announces on page 73. Digestion evidence is imprecise. Both sides introduced expert opinion. A disagreement among physicians should be presented as a disagreement, not as the complete destruction of one side’s case. The book also says Harris’s testimony laid the foundation for Dorsey to call Frank a sexual pervert. This phrasing shifts attention away from what Harris testified that he observed and toward an assumed prosecutorial strategy. A reader should be told exactly what each physician found, where they agreed, where they differed, and what limitations applied to their estimates. The book instead converts one defense opinion into an exonerating fact. Jim Conley Is Turned into a Mastermind Whenever the Narrative Requires It No careful reader should deny that Jim Conley lied during the investigation. He gave changing statements and attempted to reduce his own responsibility. The jury knew this. His earlier affidavits, inconsistencies, drinking, criminal history, and admitted falsehoods were examined at length. Luther Rosser cross-examined him for hours. The central question was not whether Conley had ever lied. It was whether the portions of his final account that implicated Frank were corroborated. The book avoids that question by transforming Conley into a highly adaptable criminal genius. He becomes intelligent enough to plan the murder, move the body, invent the notes, manipulate the police, deceive the prosecutor, withstand Rosser’s prolonged cross-examination, and exploit the racial expectations of an all-White jury. At other moments, he is presented as a frightened Black laborer whose statements were gradually constructed by police. These two Conleys are difficult to reconcile. One is the architect of the entire crime and deception. The other is an instrument in the prosecution’s campaign against Frank. The book uses whichever version best removes responsibility from Frank. The fact that police wanted additional statements from Conley does not prove that they supplied the contents. Investigators commonly confront a witness with contradictions and demand a more complete explanation. The important question is whether new details originated with Conley, whether police suggested them, and whether those details matched independently known evidence. The book treats the phrase “we wanted another statement” as nearly conclusive proof of coaching. It is not. The Will Green and William Mincey Stories Are Given More Weight Than They Deserve Page 53 introduces an unnamed carnival worker later identified as Will Green, who supposedly saw Conley attack Mary after a gambling dispute. Investigators could not locate him. He never testified. His identity, reliability, and story were never tested in court. The absence of the witness is then treated as good news for Dorsey, as though the prosecutor benefited from suppressing a dangerous eyewitness. That is speculation. An unlocated person described in a sensational newspaper story is not an eyewitness until he is found, identified, questioned, and tested. William Mincey’s alleged encounter with Conley receives similar treatment. Mincey claimed Conley confessed to killing a girl on the afternoon of April 26. Yet the defense did not call Mincey at trial. That decision is significant. Frank’s lawyers had every reason to present a credible confession by Conley. Their failure to call Mincey suggests that they had concerns about admissibility, credibility, corroboration, or the supposed supporting witnesses. The book admits that the defense never explained the omission, but still presents Mincey’s story as compelling evidence. A sound review would ask why one of Georgia’s most experienced defense teams declined to use a witness who supposedly possessed direct evidence of Conley’s guilt. Recantations and Defense Affidavits Are Treated as Established Truth The chapters concerning Minola McKnight, Dewey Hewell, and other witnesses repeatedly convert disputed later statements into proof that Dorsey manufactured the case. Minola’s treatment by police deserves serious criticism. She was detained and questioned under conditions that would be unacceptable today. Her later repudiation of her affidavit is important. It does not follow that every statement in the affidavit was false or that Dorsey invented its contents. The book uses the same approach with other witnesses. When a witness supported the prosecution in 1913 and later recanted, the recantation is treated as the true account. When the witness later withdrew or contradicted the recantation, the reversal is attributed to threats, pressure, or fear. This again creates a closed system. Statements against Frank are products of coercion. Statements for Frank are products of conscience. A later return to the original account becomes additional evidence of coercion. A reliable history must examine when each statement was made, who was present, what incentives existed, whether the person was under oath, whether cross-examination occurred, and whether independent facts supported the account. The book too often chooses the version favorable to Frank and then explains away the rest. The Racial Interpretation Is Too Simple The book argues that police and prosecutors wanted a White Yankee industrialist rather than a Black laborer because convicting Frank would be a greater achievement. It also argues that an all-White jury believed Conley because racial stereotypes made his lies seem natural and therefore credible. These are possible interpretations. The book presents them as established motives. The racial reality was more complicated. Frank’s defense asked White jurors to reject Black witnesses as liars, criminals, drunkards, and people incapable of reliable reasoning. Conley was attacked through his race as well as through his conduct. Newt Lee was subjected to severe treatment. Minola and Albert McKnight were used by both sides. Black witnesses could be treated as disposable when useful and degraded when inconvenient. Volume 3 of The Secret Relationship Between Blacks and Jews offers a strong counterargument to the conventional pro-Frank treatment of these witnesses. It asks whether modern writers who claim to oppose racism have stripped Black participants of agency by assuming they could only have acted as puppets of White prosecutors. That source is polemical and should not replace the official record. Its strongest point remains valid: a historian should evaluate what Black witnesses said, what they knew, and whether their statements were corroborated. Their testimony should not be accepted or rejected solely through racial theory. The book condemns the racism of 1913 while repeatedly explaining Black testimony as the product of ignorance, manipulation, greed, fear, or criminal cunning. That is not the respectful restoration of Black voices it may appear to be. The Circumcision Theory Is Speculation Presented as Historical Understanding Pages 69 through 71 contain one of the book’s most imaginative claims. Conley testified that Frank had said he was “not built like other men.” The book interprets this as a coded accusation that Frank’s circumcision left him sexually deformed and drove him toward unconventional sexual acts. No witness used the word circumcision. No prosecutor stated that Jewish men were anatomically deformed. No medical evidence was introduced to support such a theory. The book acknowledges that no one stated the claim openly, then proceeds to explain at length what the court supposedly understood. This is not a recovered fact. It is the author’s interpretation of an ambiguous phrase. Conley may have been referring to sexual capacity, physical weakness, reproductive anatomy, or another detail. The phrase may also have been invented. The record does not justify turning it into an unspoken courtroom theory of Jewish genital deformity. The book inserts an antisemitic argument into the trial and then condemns the prosecution for supposedly making it. The Courtroom Crowd Is Described Through an Unverified Slogan On page 61, the book states that people outside the courtroom threatened the jurors with the words, “Hang that Jew, or we’ll hang you!” That exact slogan has become one of the most frequently repeated lines in pro-Frank literature. The book’s source notes do not trace it to a stenographic court record or a clearly identified contemporary witness. They route related claims through Charles and Louise Samuels and Leonard Dinnerstein. There was hostility around the courthouse. There were demonstrations, applause, cheering, and genuine concerns about public order. Those facts should be stated accurately. An emotionally perfect quotation should not be repeated as established fact unless its origin can be identified. The distinction matters because this sentence is used to turn the jury’s decision into the result of a direct death threat. The Georgia Supreme Court reviewed allegations of disorder and the supporting and rebutting affidavits. It did not conclude that the jury had been coerced into conviction. The United States Supreme Court majority later noted that Frank’s claims had been heard repeatedly in the Georgia courts and rejected the federal habeas challenge. Justices Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. and Charles Evans Hughes dissented and believed the mob-domination allegations deserved further factual examination. Their dissent did not find Frank innocent or identify Mary’s killer. The book presents the contested constitutional argument as though it were the settled history of what happened inside the jury room. The Jury Is Replaced by a Crowd in the Narrative The trial chapters repeatedly contrast defense “facts” with prosecution “emotion.” On page 65, the book says Dorsey understood that a convincing story could not be refuted by facts. On page 73, it says defense testimony invalidated the prosecution’s entire timeline. On page 76, it claims defense witnesses systematically disproved the state’s case. On page 82, it says Arnold and Rosser effectively tore apart Dorsey’s evidence. If all of that were true, the verdict could only be explained by prejudice or fear. That is precisely how the narrative is constructed. The jury disappears as a group of twelve people evaluating weeks of testimony. It becomes an extension of the crowd. The book does not seriously consider that jurors may have believed parts of Conley’s account because they found corroboration. It does not consider that they may have found Frank’s explanations unsatisfactory, Stover credible, the physical evidence meaningful, the murder notes incriminating, or the defense theory incomplete. Instead, it repeatedly tells readers that the jurors were waiting for passion, were unmoved by reason, were impressed by theatrical arguments, and were influenced by mob law. These are conclusions about twelve men’s inner reasoning. The jurors did not leave a collective explanation of their deliberations. The verdict reveals their conclusion, not every thought that led to it. Frank’s Unsworn Statement Is Described Without Its Procedural Advantage Page 80 explains that Frank could not give sworn testimony and undergo ordinary cross-examination under Georgia’s statutory system, but could make an unsworn statement to the jury. He spoke for approximately four hours. The description is technically incomplete because it hides the strategic advantage of the procedure. Frank was permitted to tell his story directly to the jury without taking an oath and without being subjected to the same ordinary cross-examination endured by prosecution witnesses. The book portrays his lengthy discussion of pencil manufacturing and office work as evidence of an analytical personality misunderstood by emotional jurors. Another interpretation is possible. Frank concentrated upon the parts of his account he could control while avoiding hostile questioning about disputed times, his empty office, the metal room, Lee’s schedule, and contradictions in his earlier statements. Choosing the unsworn procedure did not prove guilt. It also did not make his account equivalent to testimony tested by cross-examination. The jury was entitled to consider that difference. Hugh Dorsey Is Psychologized Instead of Answered The book repeatedly explains Dorsey’s actions through personal ambition. It says he needed a major conviction to advance politically. It accuses him of building a story stronger than the facts, coercing witnesses, exploiting sexual rumor, using coded antisemitism, and suppressing evidence favorable to Frank. Some prosecutorial decisions deserve criticism. Dorsey’s methods should be tested against the record. His argument was forceful, emotional, and at times harsh. Yet the book often substitutes an accusation about motive for an answer to the evidence he presented. Dorsey did not ask jurors to believe Conley in isolation. He connected Conley’s account with Frank’s presence, Mary’s pay visit, the office timeline, Stover’s testimony, the notes, the physical evidence, Lee’s schedule, the elevator theory, the basement trail, the medical evidence, and conduct after the discovery. The book rarely reconstructs that combined argument fairly. It describes the prosecution as a web of emotion and prejudice, then congratulates the defense for cutting apart individual strands. A critic cannot disprove a cumulative case by refusing to assemble it. Judge Roan’s Doubt Is Enlarged While His Ruling Is Minimized The book gives great weight to Judge Leonard Roan’s later uncertainty about Frank’s guilt. Those remarks are important and should be included. They should also be placed beside his formal actions. On October 31, 1913, Roan denied Frank’s extensive motion for a new trial. He considered the allegations of courtroom disorder, evidentiary rulings, legal objections, and claims that the verdict was unsupported. He allowed the verdict to stand. The book treats his later discomfort almost as a judicial confession that he had upheld an unjust conviction. It gives much less emphasis to the fact that he had authority to grant a new trial and did not do so. A judge may experience personal doubt while concluding that the legal standard for disturbing a jury verdict has not been met. Doubt is not exoneration. A troubled conscience is not a finding that the defendant was innocent. The Georgia Supreme Court affirmed the conviction. Later state proceedings also failed. The book reduces this history to the suggestion that judges followed technical law rather than common sense. That is rhetoric, not legal analysis. The United States Supreme Court Decision Is Misdated and Misrepresented The timeline says the United States Supreme Court rejected Frank’s appeal on April 9, 1915. Frank v. Mangum , 237 U.S. 309, was decided on April 12, 1915. The majority affirmed the denial of federal habeas corpus relief. The Court stated that Frank had received repeated opportunities to present his claims through Georgia’s judicial system. Holmes and Hughes dissented because they believed the federal court should hear evidence concerning alleged mob domination. The dissent did not retry the murder charge. It did not declare that Conley killed Mary. It did not find Frank factually innocent. The book’s source notes contain an even larger bibliographic error, identifying the case as “237 U.S. 909” and assigning incorrect years in different entries. The correct citation is Frank v. Mangum , 237 U.S. 309 (1915). These are not obscure details. The Supreme Court proceedings are central to the book’s argument that Frank was denied due process. Tom Watson Is Projected Backward into the 1913 Trial Tom Watson later wrote vicious attacks on Frank and used unmistakably antisemitic language. His rhetoric deserves condemnation. The chronology still matters. Watson did not begin publishing about the Frank case until 1914, after the murder, investigation, indictment, trial, verdict, and initial appellate proceedings. His later campaign influenced public opinion surrounding appeals, clemency, commutation, and the aftermath. It cannot be used as direct proof that his rhetoric controlled the jury in August 1913. Pages 99 through 101 place Watson at the center of the “mob spirit” surrounding the trial without maintaining that chronological distinction. The reader is left with the impression that his published campaign helped produce the original conviction. Later hatred cannot simply be projected backward and used to explain an earlier verdict. Governor Slaton Is Presented as the Only Clear-Sighted Authority The treatment of Governor John M. Slaton is openly heroic. The book calls him a man of conscience and says he was the only person in authority willing to ignore emotion and look clearly at the case. Other officials are portrayed as fearful, ambitious, prejudiced, or trapped by legal technicalities. Slaton alone sees the truth. This is hagiography, not balanced history. Slaton conducted a substantial review and issued a detailed commutation statement. His decision deserves careful study. It also deserves context. His law firm had joined with the firm of Luther Rosser, Frank’s lead trial attorney, at the opening of Slaton’s gubernatorial term. That relationship does not prove that the commutation was corrupt. It was politically and ethically significant enough that a balanced account should examine it directly rather than presenting Slaton as a detached outsider. The book also relies upon disputed affidavits, reported confessions, late statements, and material never tested before the trial jury as though Slaton’s consideration transformed them into proven evidence. A commutation is an executive act of mercy or sentence reduction. Slaton changed Frank’s punishment from death to life imprisonment. He did not overturn the conviction, order a new trial, or declare Frank innocent. The timeline dates the commutation to June 20, 1915. Slaton’s formal order was dated June 21, 1915. The Lynching Was Criminal, but It Did Not Prove Innocence Frank’s abduction and lynching on August 17, 1915, were criminal and indefensible. The men who removed him from state custody denied him the protection of law. Georgia failed to protect a prisoner and failed to prosecute his killers. No conclusion about Frank’s guilt can excuse those acts. The book’s account of the lynching is among its strongest sections. It describes the organization of the abductors, the journey to Milledgeville, the removal of Frank, the return to Cobb County, the hanging, and the public reaction. Even here, factual and interpretive problems remain. A photograph on page 120 is captioned as showing that Frank was lynched on the morning of August 16. He was abducted during the night of August 16 and hanged on the morning of August 17. The text also assigns thoughts and meanings to Frank’s last statements. It suggests that his calmness, concern for his wife, and refusal to confess reflected innocence. Those actions may show courage, loyalty, self-control, or innocence. They do not prove which person killed Mary Phagan. A wrongful lynching and a wrongful conviction are separate claims. The first is established. The second remains disputed. The book repeatedly allows the horror of the lynching to flow backward and erase the evidence from the trial. The Anti-Defamation League Claim Is False Pages 124 and 125 state that, after Frank’s lynching, his supporters worked to form the Anti-Defamation League of B’nai B’rith. A caption says the lynching led to the founding of the ADL. The ADL was founded in 1913, two years before Frank’s death. The organization itself has clarified that the Frank case was not the impetus for its founding. Sigmund Livingston had conceived the organization before the case. The trial later reinforced the perceived need for an organization opposing antisemitism, but it did not cause the ADL to be created after the lynching. This is an especially serious error in a book intended to teach history to young readers. The page includes a photograph of a newspaper dated in 1913, which should have alerted the author and editors that the organization existed before August 1915. The Book Oversimplifies the Rebirth of the Ku Klux Klan The same pages state that the Knights of Mary Phagan “reestablished the Ku Klux Klan” and that Frank’s lynching led to the Klan’s reemergence. There was a connection between the Frank controversy and the second Klan. Some men associated with the new order had also been associated with a group described as the Knights of Mary Phagan. Antisemitism arising from the case formed part of the political atmosphere. The book reduces a complicated historical development to a direct act of organizational succession. William Joseph Simmons founded the second Klan in 1915. D. W. Griffith’s The Birth of a Nation , fraternal-order culture, White supremacy, anti-Catholicism, antisemitism, nativism, and the Frank controversy all contributed to the environment. On Thanksgiving night in 1915, Simmons and sixteen other men gathered at Stone Mountain. Several, not necessarily all, had ties to the Knights of Mary Phagan. The book turns influence into sole causation and a disputed organization into the direct founder of a national movement. A young reader will leave with a memorable sentence, but not an accurate understanding of how the second Klan developed. Alonzo Mann Is Called an Eyewitness When He Was a Late Claimant The final chapters depend heavily upon Alonzo Mann’s 1982 affidavit. Mann was eighty-three years old when he claimed that, sixty-nine years earlier, he had entered the factory and seen Conley carrying Mary’s body near the trapdoor. He said Conley threatened him and that his mother ordered him to remain silent. The book calls Mann “the last eyewitness.” He was not an eyewitness to the murder. At most, he claimed to have witnessed Conley carrying the body. That distinction is crucial. Conley had already admitted carrying Mary’s body. Seeing him with the body would contradict parts of his trial account, particularly the location and method of transport. It would not automatically prove that Frank had no role in the killing or cover-up. Mann’s delay also demands serious skepticism. He remained silent during the investigation, coroner’s inquest, trial, motions for a new trial, state appeals, federal proceedings, clemency campaign, Slaton review, and the decades of public controversy that followed. He was never cross-examined about the 1982 account. Investigators could no longer question Conley, Mann’s parents, Frank, the trial lawyers, or most people who had been inside the building. The book says Mann passed two polygraph examinations and treats this as confirmation that he told the truth. Polygraph results are not scientific proof that a historical recollection is accurate. A person may sincerely believe a distorted or reconstructed memory. The book goes further and says Mann’s account could have exonerated Frank and convicted Conley. That conclusion exceeds what the affidavit establishes. Even the 1986 pardon did not adopt Mann’s account as proof of innocence. The 1986 Pardon Is Quoted Correctly but Framed Misleadingly To its credit, the book reproduces the central language of the 1986 pardon. The board expressly stated that it was acting “without attempting to address the question of guilt or innocence.” The pardon recognized Georgia’s failure to protect Frank while he remained in state custody, its failure to preserve his opportunity for continued legal action, and its failure to prosecute his killers. That was a humanitarian pardon. It was not an exoneration. Yet the surrounding chapter places the pardon after Mann’s affidavit, the supposed Conley confession, and other innocence claims. The narrative design encourages readers to treat the pardon as the official conclusion of an innocence campaign. The board deliberately refused to reach that conclusion. The exact language remains controlling. The first pardon application, which more directly implied innocence, was denied on December 22, 1983. The second succeeded because it rested upon the state’s failures surrounding the lynching, not upon a finding that Frank had been wrongly convicted. The A. L. Henson Story Is Untested Hearsay Page 131 says attorney A. L. Henson claimed that Conley confessed to struggling with a girl in the pencil factory and later finding himself in the basement with her dead body. This account appeared decades after the case in Henson’s memoir. Conley was not available for examination. The supposed conversation was not recorded at the time, presented at trial, or tested through cross-examination. The book treats attorney-client privilege as the reason Henson remained silent. That explanation does not transform the story into reliable evidence. It is another example of the book’s unequal standards. A late statement against Conley is accepted as meaningful. Contemporary testimony against Frank is placed under suspicion. Pierre van Paassen’s Legends Dominate the Conclusion Pages 132 and 133 return to van Paassen’s bite-mark story and add further dramatic allegations. The book says he tried to publish proof that Frank’s teeth did not match the wounds. It says someone warned him to abandon the case. It then recounts his claim that a large automobile forced him into the path of a streetcar. These events are presented in smooth narrative prose without independent corroboration. The effect is powerful. The reader imagines hidden forensic evidence, a corrupt prosecutor, threatening messages, and an attempted murder intended to preserve the conspiracy. The proof remains one man’s memoir, published in 1964, concerning events he said occurred in 1922. The book criticizes the 1913 jury for accepting unreliable testimony while using a much lower standard for evidence supporting Frank. The Final Chapters Treat Speculation as Resolution By page 132, the book is no longer asking whether factory witnesses lied. It asks why so many of them lied. That wording assumes the conclusion. It suggests peer pressure, desire for attention, coercion, emotional mass hysteria, and collective delusion. The possibility that some witnesses gave substantially truthful testimony is largely removed. Page 133 asks how a suspect can defend himself when the justice system has been corrupted. Again, corruption is no longer a proposition to be demonstrated. It is the foundation of the question. Page 134 closes with the tenderness of Lucille’s loyalty, the admiration of Frank’s lawyers, and the determination of legal minds to correct injustice. The facing pages then place Mary’s epitaph beside a marker declaring Frank “wrongly accused” and “falsely convicted.” The visual and verbal argument is complete. Mary and Frank are placed together as paired victims, but Frank receives the final declaration of innocence. The book has not proven that declaration. It has arranged the story so that the reader feels it. The Timeline and Reference Material Contain Numerous Errors The timeline and reference sections should have been the easiest parts of the book to verify. They contain a surprising number of mistakes. The book gives May 23, 1913, as the date of Frank’s indictment. The indictment was returned on May 24. It gives April 9, 1915, as the date of the United States Supreme Court decision. The decision was issued on April 12. It says Frank’s execution was rescheduled for June 22, 1916. The correct year was 1915. It places Slaton’s commutation on June 20 rather than June 21. It dates William Creen’s attack to July 17, 1815, an obvious typographical error. It dates the 1986 pardon to March 11, 1985. It identifies Mary in the major-figures section as having been murdered on April 26, 1918. The photograph caption on page 120 dates the lynching to the morning of August 16 rather than August 17. The source notes give an incorrect United States Reports citation for Frank v. Mangum and attach incorrect years to the case. These errors do not all carry equal historical importance. Together, they weaken confidence in a book that asks readers to trust its correction of a complicated legal history. The Photographs Are the Book’s Strongest Feature The book’s greatest value lies in its visual presentation. It contains photographs of Mary Phagan, Leo and Lucille Frank, the National Pencil Company building, lawyers, investigators, jurors, newspapers, the prison farm, the lynching site, and many other people and places connected with the case. The production values are high, and several photographs are reproduced more clearly than in older works. The captions, however, must be checked independently. As the incorrect lynching date demonstrates, a well-reproduced photograph can still carry misleading information. The images make the book worth examining. They do not make the surrounding narrative dependable. Why Mary Phagan-Kean’s Revised Edition Is a Better Starting Point Readers seeking to understand the case should begin with Mary Phagan-Kean’s substantially expanded 2025 edition of The Murder of Little Mary Phagan . Phagan-Kean writes from the Phagan family’s perspective and openly believes that the evidence supports Frank’s conviction. She does not pretend to occupy a position without personal or historical commitments. Her revised work is still a better introduction because it restores the subject that this book gradually displaces: Mary Phagan, the investigation of her murder, the testimony heard at trial, the physical evidence, the appeals, and the difference between conviction, commutation, lynching, pardon, and exoneration. It also requires readers to confront evidence frequently omitted or minimized in pro-Frank accounts. This includes Newt Lee’s changed schedule, the time slip, the murder notes, Monteen Stover’s testimony, Frank’s shifting explanation of the noon period, the second-floor evidence, the basement route, medical testimony, and the extensive appellate record. Phagan-Kean’s conclusions should be tested against the primary sources, just as every other historian’s conclusions should be tested. Her work provides a much fuller foundation from which to begin that comparison. Additional counterpoints include Arthur Burton Rascoe’s The Case of Leo Frank , Francis Xavier Busch’s chapter in Guilty or Not Guilty? , Tom W. Brown’s Notes on the Case of Leo M. Frank and Its Aftermath , and Volume 3 of The Secret Relationship Between Blacks and Jews . Tom Watson’s writings also preserve parts of the contemporary pro-verdict argument, but his antisemitic and inflammatory rhetoric must be separated from any factual or legal claims. His language is not evidence. No secondary book should replace the 1913 Brief of Evidence , the motions and appellate records, the contemporary Atlanta newspapers, the surviving prosecution and defense arguments, and the official pardon decisions. Final Assessment An Unspeakable Crime is not a good book from which to learn the Leo Frank case, it is defense agitprop. It is useful for understanding how the modern pro-Frank narrative is presented to young readers. It shows how Frank can be transformed from a convicted defendant into the central victim of Mary Phagan’s murder story. Its method is consistent. Mary’s biography is handled carelessly. Frank’s biography is enlarged sympathetically. Weak evidence favoring Frank is accepted. Stronger evidence against him is fragmented or omitted. Dorsey’s motives are attacked. The jurors’ thoughts are invented. Late recantations are elevated, but no mention of how they were induced is mentioned. Contemporary testimony is distrusted. Executive commutation is treated as moral vindication. A humanitarian pardon is positioned near exoneration. The criminal injustice of the lynching is allowed to erase the unresolved question of factual guilt. The book’s author plainly researched the case and visited important archives. The problem was not an absence of effort. It was the direction of that effort. She entered the research already convinced that Frank had suffered a travesty of justice, then organized the surviving record around that conviction. Its strongly partisan pro-Frank perspective leads it to emphasize information that supports its conclusion while giving insufficient attention to evidence that complicates or challenges that interpretation. The book belongs beside Leonard Dinnerstein, Harry Golden, and Charles and Louise Samuels as part of an established tradition of extreme pro-Frank advocacy. It does not introduce readers to the full controversy. It initiates them into one side of it. Its clear prose, striking photographs, and attractive design may give the impression of authority, but the numerous factual mistakes, unsupported legends, selective source use, imagined motives, chronological errors, and missing prosecution evidence tell a different story. The photographs introduce the faces. The narrative has already assigned the halos and horns. The essential rule for studying the case should be simple: establish the facts first, then form the interpretation. An Unspeakable Crime too often reverses that order, selecting the information that best supports its argument while giving insufficient scrutiny to claims that are disputed, weakly sourced, or unsupported by the surviving record. results.title: The Travels Of Reverend Olafur Egilsson
results.creator: Ólafur Egilsson (Author), Karl Smári Hreinsson (Editor), Adam Nichols (Editor, Translator), Karl Smari Hreinsson (Translator)
results.description: A seventeenth-century minister tells his story of abduction by pirates, and a solo journey from Algiers to Copenhagen, in this remarkable historical text.   In summer 1627, Barbary corsairs raided Iceland, killing dozens and abducting almost four hundred people to sell into slavery in Algiers. Among those taken was Lutheran minister Olafur Egilsson.   Reverend Olafur—born in the same year as William Shakespeare and Galileo Galilei—wrote  The Travels  to chronicle his experiences both as a captive and as a traveler across Europe as he journeyed alone from Algiers to Copenhagen in an attempt to raise funds to ransom the Icelandic captives that remained behind. He was a keen observer, and the narrative is filled with a wealth of detail―social, political, economic, religious―about both the Maghreb and Europe. It is also a moving story on the human level: We witness a man enduring great personal tragedy and struggling to reconcile such calamity with his understanding of God.   The Travels  is the first-ever English translation of the Icelandic text. Until now, the corsair raid on Iceland has remained largely unknown in the English-speaking world. To give a clearer sense of the extraordinary events connected with that raid, this edition of  The Travels  includes not only Reverend Olafur’s first-person narrative but also a collection of contemporary letters describing both the events of the raid itself and the conditions under which the enslaved Icelanders lived. Also included are appendices containing background information on the cities of Algiers and Salé in the seventeenth century, on Iceland in the seventeenth century, on the manuscripts accessed for the translation, and on the book’s early modern European context.

results.title: The Regency Of Algiers
results.creator: Thomas J. Bryan, Claude/Anthropic
results.description: The Regency of Algiers: Patterns of Power (1516–1830) is an analytical case study examining how an order of power was founded, dressed, and held across three centuries . The study follows the state's trajectory from the seizure of Algiers by the corsair brothers Aruj and Khayr al-Din , through its submission to the Ottoman sultan and the eventual rise of the janissary corporation , to the capitulation of the Kasba to a French army on July 5, 1830 . Relying on primary administrative records, consular testimonies, eyewitness accounts, and period inscriptions , the work investigates an order whose revenue ran through maritime and state chokepoints , governed by a corporation that recruited free adult volunteers abroad while barring native Algerians from its pay registers and highest ranks . The volume explores the mechanics of an institutional arrangement where individual titles—such as places on the pay register, prize shares, and farmed offices—were strictly non-heritable and died with their holders , yet the corporate system itself endured . Rather than treating the Regency simply through the conventional lens of a "pirate state," the study details its administrative realities: the extraction of surplus via monopolies, tribute, and escheat ; the dual claims of holy war and diplomatic treaty under Ottoman safe-conduct ; the complete separation between local religious formation and state governance ; and the structural forces that eventually hollowed the order prior to the 1830 conquest .

results.title: Pirates of Barbary : corsairs, conquests, and captivity in the seventeenth-century Mediterranean
results.creator: Tinniswood, Adrian
description: It's easy to think of piracy as a romantic way of life long gone--if not for today's headlines of robbery and kidnapping on the high seas. Pirates have existed since the invention of commerce itself, but they reached the zenith of their power during the 1600s, when the Mediterranean was the crossroads of the world, and pirates were the scourge of Europe and the glory of Islam. They attacked ships, enslaved crews, plundered cargoes, enraged governments, and swayed empires. Historian Adrian Tinniswood brings alive this chapter in history, where clashes between pirates of the East--Tunis, Algiers, and Tripoli--and governments of the West--England, France, Spain, and Venice--grew increasingly intense and dangerous, and he shows how their maneuverings between the Muslim empires and Christian Europe shed light on the religious and moral battles that still rage today.--From publisher description

results.title: The moral consequences of economic growth
results.creator: Friedman, Benjamin M
description: x, 570 pages ; 25 cm

""Are we right," Benjamin M. Friedman asks, "to care so much about economic growth as we clearly do?" To answer, Friedman reaches beyond economics. He examines the political and social histories of the large Western democracies - particularly of the United States since the Civil War - distinguishing times of generally rising living standards from those of pervasive stagnation to illustrate how rising incomes render a society more open and democratic. He shows, too, how our attitudes toward economic growth and its consequences have roots in the thinking of prior centuries, especially the Enlightenment, and also include significant strands of religious influence." "Friedman also delineates the role of economic growth in determining which developing nations extend the broadest freedoms to their citizenry. He makes clear that growth, rather than just the level of living standards, is key to effecting political and social liberalization in the third world. But he also warns that the democratic values of countries even as wealthy as our own are at risk whenever incomes stagnate for extended periods. Merely being rich is no protection against a society's retreat into rigidity and intolerance once enough of its citizens lose the sense that they are getting ahead." "Finally, Friedman shows us why, if America is to strengthen democratic institutions around the world as a bulwark against terrorism and social unrest, we must aggressively pursue growth at home and promote worldwide economic expansion beyond what purely market-driven forces would create. And for the United States, he offers concrete suggestions for policy steps to achieve those objectives."--Jacket
Includes bibliographical references and index
